4429.prule: Main stress falls on the final syllable of the prosodic word (the 'main syllable'); any preceding syllable is an unstressed presyllable. 4436.dloc: Section 2.4 'Stress', p. 413 (the whole section sits on this page, 2.5 Phonotactics opens p. 414); scope statement section 2.1 p. 407; language inventory section 1.4 p. 403 (language (f)); west-coast consonant-final remark section 2.5 p. 414.
4436.prule: No rule fixed. Working from 19th-century recorders' accent diacritics (Walker, Norman), Milligan's orthographic remark, Tindale's transcriptions, the Fanny Cochrane Smith cylinders and Crowley's 1972 recordings, the authors infer, hedged ('it appears'), that disyllables are stressed on the first syllable and trisyllables on the first or the second syllable with no conditioning given; their 'only general conclusion' is negative: any syllable except the last can bear stress. Stated for 'Tasmanian' collectively; p. 407 says the phonology 'is based mainly on the mid-eastern and south-eastern languages... It seems likely that most of our remarks will also apply to languages in other parts of Tasmania'. None of the six evidence sources is specifically north-western (Milligan's vocabularies include some two hundred words 'assigned to north-west and western tribes', which Crowley and Dixon say correspond poorly with earlier vocabularies from those areas, p. 397); nothing stress-specific is said about language (f).

4444.dq: Stress is marked after the syllable; the main stress is marked with " e.g. do"ki; secondary stress is marked witn ' e.g. tam"baya' (last syllable). (The examples are isolated words and the 'Tone and Stress of the Past Tense' section lists verb forms by syllable count, but the source never states a domain or contrasts word with phrase prominence.)

4444.prule: No positional stress rule. In Abraham's 1929 Hausa-modelled, pre-phonemic analysis 'stress' is a notational derivative of the tone melody: §29 (p. 114) equates stressed syllables with High tone and unstressed with Low, and in his own transcriptions (p. 205, read) the main-stress mark (") always sits after a syllable bearing the highest tone level present in the word (High if any, otherwise Mid: go"woyi' High, Low, Mid; indu"wo Low, Mid, Low; fullu"woyi' Low, Mid, Low, Mid; laduruŋ"go Low, Low, Mid, Low; sikitu"woyi' Low, Low, Mid, Low, Mid), though not necessarily after the first such syllable (mo"tu'wo and du"ru'wo High, High, Low, but wo'du"woyi' High, High, Low, Mid), and the secondary mark (') after the other non-Low syllables, whether High (mo"tu'wo) or Mid (go"woyi'). Placement therefore follows the lexical/grammatical tone melody, not syllable count or weight. Modern descriptions (Gimba 1998, 2000; Gimba, Ali, Bah & Schuh 2009; Schuh 2005) treat Bole as a two-tone (H/L) register language with downdrift, tone spreading and Low Tone Raising, and never mention stress.
4444.srule: Abraham 1929 names and marks a 'secondary stress' (') but gives no placement rule ('secondary stress is marked witn ' e.g. tam"baya' (last syllable)', p. 204); in his transcriptions the mark follows the non-Low syllables other than the main-stressed one (go"woyi' H-L-M, mo"tu'wo H-H-L, p. 205; Past-tense pronoun suffixes 'all have stress except -ni which has Low Tone', p. 214), i.e. it is a tone correlate. Superseded: Schuh, Gimba & Ritchart 2010 (pp. 226, 235) find no lexical or phrasal stress in Bole, hence no secondary stress.

4447.prule: Mixed 'tono acentual' system ('stress to high tone', Wetzels & Meira). Lexical tone contrast on monosyllabic lexemes: L (default, unmarked) vs HL vs LH; a polysyllabic morpheme carries at most one H (contour split left-to-right over the first two syllables). Intensity stress is predictable and non-contrastive: in bi- and trisyllabic monomorphemic words it falls on the syllable bearing H; when the word has no H it falls on the first syllable from the left. Since H sits on the first syllable in most such words (H.L, H.L.L; L.L and L.L.L stressed initially), stress is in effect word-initial and demarcates the prosodic word; the author says this 'could be interpreted as a fixed, non-contrastive stress' (p.233).

4453.heavy: 'either a long vowel or a vowel-sonorant sequence consist of two moras' (p. 59): heavy = long vowel (V:) or short vowel + tautosyllabic sonorant/nasal coda; 'when there is an obstruent in the coda, there is no effect on the placement of stress' (p. 59); VʔV sequences 'behave as a single, long vowel' and may outrank heavy syllables (p. 60).

4453.prule: Primary stress is confined to the first two syllables of the word (the initial foot). Stress the leftmost heavy syllable within that window; if both are light, stress the first. So: #H́L, #H́H, #ĹL, #LH́. Heavy = long vowel, or short vowel plus a tautosyllabic sonorant (nasal) coda; obstruent codas are irrelevant; long vowels beyond the second syllable never take primary stress.
4453.srule: Secondary stresses occur beyond the initial foot; Stonham tentatively places them on alternating syllables counted from the primary stress, following the disyllabic foot structure, and says their placement 'remains to be clearly worked out'. The first vowel of a VʔV sequence attracts (primary or secondary) stress anywhere in the word.
